title: Innovation spaces: Workspace planning and innovation in U.S. university research centers
research_question: 1. What method of consultation do scientists use to obtain technical information? a. What method of obtaining technical information do scientists prefer? 2. To what extent do individual spatial variables predict consultations within URCS? a. What are the net or multivariate effects of significant individual spatial variables on consultations within URCs? 3. Across URCs, what is the relationship of overall workspace planning approaches to consultations? 4. Across URCs, what is the relationship between overall workspace planning approaches and innovation process outcomes?

participants.description: 85 scientists (82% response rate) working in six U.S. University Research Centers (URCs). URCs were organizationally similar (strategic basic/use-based research, funding structure, reporting structure, number of scientists, scientific focus mostly genetics/genomics/biology).
participants.recruitment: 104 scientists working with the six selected URCs were asked to participate; 85 completed the study instruments.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Six U.S. University Research Centers (URCs) with different workspace planning approaches: two intact with laboratories, two non-intact with laboratories, and two intact without laboratories. Spatial characteristics (configurational accessibility, visibility, walking distances) were measured from floor plans.
Floor plans of the six URCs were used to calculate spatial variables (global integration, intelligibility, visibility, walking distances) using space syntax and visibility graph analysis software.

measures.instrument: Week-long activity log (scientists recorded initiated consultations, location, type)
Activity log categories: unscheduled office visits, coincidental consultations, prescheduled office visits, prescheduled group meetings, unscheduled group meetings, intra-URC e-mails, telephone calls
Social network analysis (sum of relational ties / total possible ties)
Follow-up survey (reported number of books, articles, papers, project proposals, patents, etc., standardized per scientist per month)
Follow-up survey (7-point Likert scale on 'creativity and innovativeness', 'overall contribution', 'recognition/reputation', 'overall satisfaction')
Follow-up survey (priority ratings for nine information resources)
Visibility graph analysis software (area seen from each space)
Measured from floor plans (actual distance in feet)

mechanisms: Configurational accessibility of common spaces increases the number of paths between spaces, leading to more opportunities for bumping into other scientists.
High visibility in common spaces increases the chances for eye-to-eye contact, facilitating discussions.
Shorter walking distances between spaces increase the frequency of chance encounters.
Segregated offices and laboratories in non-intact territories lead to lower overall configurational accessibility and longer walking distances, inhibiting face-to-face consultations.
Scientists in configurationally and visually segregated offices tend to substitute e-media for face-to-face consultations.
Intact URCs with laboratories may increase travel within the territory (between offices and labs), increasing unprogrammed encounters.
Face-to-face consultation and network connectivity mediate the effect of workspace arrangements on innovation outcomes.
moderators: Role of key communicators (influences the strength of spatial factors on unscheduled office visits)
implementation_implications: The built environment significantly influences human behavior and encounters, with important consequences for research settings.
Workspace design effects are determined by a complex interplay of overall planning approach, configurational properties, walking distance, and visibility of common rooms.

Non-intact URC territories (segregated offices/labs, long walking distances, decreased configurational accessibility, non-territorial connections) inhibit face-to-face consultations and lead to innovation-related losses.
Strategic workspace planning focused on facilitating face-to-face consultations is more advantageous than planning based solely on cost reduction or equipment efficiency.
Policy makers should consider micro-level workspace planning in publicly funded research settings (like URCs) as a tool to foster information flow, collaboration, and innovation.
R&D workspaces should provide a variety of environments (informal, ad hoc, private, formal meeting spaces) to accommodate both interaction and concentrated work/privacy needs.

limitations: Limited body of existing research on workspace design-innovation links.
Previous studies often failed to identify all relevant factors (e.g., visibility, non-face-to-face media).
Previous studies lacked multivariate analyses, potentially overstating bivariate relationships.
Causal relationships between workspace design, consultations, and innovation outcomes are not yet clear or certain.
Previous studies often examined constructs at a global level, not differentiating types of interactions (e.g., coincidental vs. preprogrammed).
Contexts of previous studies (e.g., energy utility, advertising companies) may not be representative of innovation settings.
Failure in previous literature to examine workspace, consultations, and innovation process outcomes within a single study.
Small sample size (N=6 URCs) limits statistical power and generalizability.
Cross-sectional design limits causal inference; longitudinal designs are needed.
Need for more sophisticated statistical tools like hierarchical linear modeling to unravel relative importance of factors.
Need to improve sampling of research days and encounters (e.g., random sampling).
Need to increase diversity and validity of innovation process and outcome measures.
Need to expand the types of URCs and research settings studied (e.g., social sciences, humanities, different national contexts).
Need to estimate the relative contribution of spatial factors compared to social and cognitive factors (e.g., culture, team compatibility, leadership, creativity).

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Physical proximity and workspace design influence the frequency and quality of spontaneous social interactions among researchers.
Workspace design impacts communication patterns, including formal and informal information exchange, which are crucial for knowledge sharing.
Effective knowledge sharing and collaboration are critical antecedents to innovation in research environments.
